BXL-2425-00023-v1.headline: Make airlines pay for their CO2: approve the deal between Belgium's governments that puts flying into the EU carbon market and phases out airlines' free pollution permits.
BXL-2425-00023-v1.proposed_by: Brussels Capital Region Government (minister Alain Maron); co-signed by the federal State, Walloon Region, Flemish Region
BXL-2425-00023-v1.source_brief:
Aviation is one of the most carbon-intensive and hardest-to-decarbonise sectors: aircraft fuel is not subject to excise duties, low-cost and private jet traffic keeps growing, and electric or hydrogen aircraft remain years away. This ordinance gives the Brussels Parliament's assent to the revised inter-federal cooperation agreement that updates Belgium's implementation of the EU Emissions Trading System for aviation under the EU's Fit for 55 package.

- **What changes:** free emissions allowances for airlines are progressively abolished, the ETS is extended to all intra-European flights, and the international CORSIA offset mechanism is integrated into Belgian law.
- **The constitutional step:** because aviation is a shared federal-regional competence, all four Belgian entities must each pass an assent ordinance; Brussels is acting on the text agreed by the National Climate Commission.
- **The delay:** the transposition was due by end of 2023; the parliament is catching up after the National Climate Commission finalised the texts and addressed remarks from the Council of State.
- **The rub:** supporters see this as a necessary polluter-pays step and a level playing field for airlines; critics argue the ETS is a market mechanism that lets big polluters buy their way out of real change, that CORSIA offset projects almost never deliver genuine emission reductions, and that aviation still enjoys far cheaper travel costs than rail alternatives.
deep_facts: The ordinance (dossier A-99, nos A-99/1, 2 et 3 – 2024/2025) gives Brussels Capital Region's assent to the cooperation agreement of 4 April 2024, which amends the original cooperation agreement of 2 September 2013 on aviation in the EU ETS; the texts were reported to the plenary by rapporteur Mounir Laarissi (CRI, 28 May 2025).

The reform is part of the EU Fit for 55 package targeting at least 55% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 relative to 1990 levels; the Brussels ordinance is one of several parallel assent texts required across all Belgian federated entities because aviation straddles federal and regional competences (CRI, 28 May 2025).

Key changes introduced by the revised agreement: (1) progressive abolition of free CO2 allowances for the aviation sector; (2) extension of the EU ETS to intra-European flights; (3) integration of the CORSIA (Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation) international offset mechanism into Belgian law (CRI, 28 May 2025).

The transposition should have been completed by end of 2023; the delay was attributed to the complexity of the inter-federal coordination; the National Climate Commission examined remarks from the Council of State before finalising the texts, and the minister stated those concerns were fully addressed in the environment committee (CRI, 28 May 2025).

Minister Alain Maron identified several reasons aviation is a climate policy weak point: no excise taxes on aviation fuel; continued sector growth with more flights and airports seeking expansion (including Zaventem, Liège and Charleroi); private jets; and the near-term unavailability of electric or hydrogen aircraft (CRI, 28 May 2025).

The PTB group opposed the text, arguing the ETS is a market mechanism allowing large multinationals to buy the right to keep polluting rather than structurally changing their practices; PTB cited studies suggesting only 2% of CORSIA offset projects result in genuine emission reductions, and called instead for massive rail investment, strict rules on short-haul flights, removal of aviation fiscal privileges and a ban on private jets (CRI, 28 May 2025).

Several speakers noted the contradiction between phasing in carbon pricing for aviation while Flanders and Wallonia simultaneously renew and expand airport environmental permits — the minister acknowledged that all policy levels should align their approaches (CRI, 28 May 2025).

Multiple groups (MR, Les Engagés, Ecolo, PS, DéFI, cd&v, Team Fouad Ahidar) stressed that making flights more expensive only makes climate sense if accompanied by massive investment in international and domestic rail, so that sustainable alternatives are available and affordable (CRI, 28 May 2025).

The ETS principle, as explained by the minister, is not simply to let industries buy pollution rights indefinitely: CO2 quotas decrease over time, making each tonne of emissions progressively costlier, which is designed to create a structural economic incentive to decarbonise; a number of previously free quotas are eliminated under this revised agreement (CRI, 28 May 2025).
BXL-2425-00023-v1.deep_lectura:
**Analyst read** *(inference — not stated verbatim in the record)*

- The broad cross-party yes vote (with only PTB's 15 voting against) reflects this being a compliance obligation rather than a choice: Belgium had no option but to transpose EU law, and Brussels could not unilaterally block or reshape the cooperation agreement, which meant most groups could vote yes without fully endorsing ETS as climate strategy.
- The PTB dissent is structurally coherent — opposing market-based mechanisms on principle — but it also serves a political function of differentiating PTB from the rest when the practical outcome (the text passing) was never in doubt.
- The airport-expansion contradiction raised by the minister points at the real political limit of the instrument: carbon pricing through ETS is a federal-European mechanism, while permitting decisions that drive traffic growth sit with Wallonia and Flanders, meaning Brussels can assent to pricing but cannot close the loop on volume.
- CORSIA is the most contested element in the room: integrating a mechanism whose environmental integrity is heavily disputed into Belgian law while the EU and ICAO continue to debate its adequacy suggests the legal compliance frame is doing more work than the climate accountability frame in this vote.
BXL-2425-00023-v1.raw_fr: L'ordonnance donne l'assentiment de la Région de Bruxelles-Capitale à l'accord de coopération du 4 avril 2024, qui modifie l'accord de 2013 relatif à l'intégration des activités aériennes dans le système communautaire d'échange de quotas d'émission (EU ETS), dans le cadre du paquet européen « ajustement à l'objectif 55 ». Les principales modifications portent sur la suppression progressive des quotas gratuits pour l'aviation, l'extension du système aux vols intraeuropéens et l'intégration du mécanisme international Corsia en droit belge. La transposition, qui aurait dû intervenir fin 2023, a été finalisée par la Commission nationale climat après examen des observations du Conseil d'État.
